claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The panD gene may be used as a potential target to control systemic Salmonella infection.
claims.source: Considering that the panD gene is present in the genomes of all Salmonella strains and that mutation of panD markedly reduced Salmonella replication ability in macrophages, as well as virulence in the mouse model, this gene may be used as a potential target to control systemic Salmonella infection.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the potential application of the findings.

results.result: Targeted metabolomics analysis of Salmonella-infected macrophages revealed that β-alanine concentrations were significantly downregulated compared to mock-infected macrophages. Eight amino acids showed significant differences in abundance between the two groups, with β-alanine being one of five downregulated amino acids.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C25 and C29 are supported by LC-MS/MS metabolomics data presented in Figure 1C-D with appropriate statistical criteria (VIP >1, p<0.05, FC >1.5 or <0.667). The experimental design includes biological replicates (n=4) and proper controls (mock-infected vs. infected). The PCA analysis (C23, Figure 1B) demonstrates clear separation between groups, supporting the validity of the metabolomics approach.

results.result: Exogenous β-alanine supplementation (1-4 mM) significantly enhanced Salmonella intracellular replication in RAW264.7 macrophages in a dose-dependent manner, suggesting that Salmonella utilizes host-derived β-alanine for intracellular growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 are directly supported by experimental data in Figure 1E showing dose-dependent increases in bacterial replication with statistical significance (p<0.001). Claims C30, C33, and C37 are reasonable inferences from the combined metabolomics (decreased β-alanine in infected cells) and supplementation data. The experiments include appropriate replicates (n=3) and controls.

results.result: Addition of 1 mM β-alanine to Salmonella-infected macrophages did not affect ROS/RNS levels or the percentage of M1/M2 macrophages, indicating that β-alanine does not alter the macrophage immune response.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplements 1-2 showing no significant differences in ROS/RNS levels or M1/M2 macrophage percentages. Claim C36 is a reasonable inference from these data. The experiments include appropriate replicates (n=3) and proper controls, ruling out indirect effects of β-alanine on macrophage antimicrobial activity.

results.result: Unlike E. coli, Salmonella does not use CycA as a β-alanine transporter. The ΔcycA mutant retained the ability to use β-alanine as a sole carbon source and showed no defects in intracellular replication or mouse colonization.
results.evaluation: Claims C39, C41-C42 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplements 3-6 showing that the ΔcycA mutant has no growth defect with β-alanine and no virulence attenuation. Claim C40 is a valid inference from these data. Claim C38 is supported by citation. The experiments include appropriate controls and statistical analyses (n=5 mice per group for in vivo studies).

results.result: GabP, which transports the β-alanine structural analog GABA in E. coli, is not involved in β-alanine uptake in Salmonella. The ΔgabP mutant showed no growth defect in minimal medium with β-alanine as the sole carbon source.
results.evaluation: Claim C44 is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplements 7-8. Claim C45 is a valid inference from these data. Claim C43 is supported by citation to Pavić et al., 2021. The experimental approach is appropriate for testing transporter function, with proper controls and replicates (n=3).

results.result: The ΔargT mutant showed markedly decreased growth in minimal medium with β-alanine as the sole carbon source, suggesting that ArgT transports β-alanine in Salmonella.
results.evaluation: Claim C46 is supported by experimental data in Figure 1F showing decreased growth of the ΔargT mutant. Claim C47 is a reasonable inference from these data. However, the conclusion would be strengthened by complementation experiments and direct transport assays. The experiment includes appropriate controls and replicates (n=4).

results.result: Expression of the panD gene (encoding L-aspartate decarboxylase) was significantly upregulated in Salmonella growing inside RAW264.7 macrophages and in N-minimal medium compared to rich medium, suggesting a relationship between panD expression and intracellular growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 are supported by qRT-PCR and bioluminescent reporter data in Figure 2B-D with statistical significance (p<0.01). Claims C52-C53 are reasonable inferences from these data. The experiments include appropriate biological replicates (n=3) and proper controls. N-minimal medium is an established model for intracellular conditions.

results.result: The ΔpanD mutant showed a 2.4-fold reduction in replication in RAW264.7 macrophages at 20 hr post-infection compared to wild-type, with significantly fewer bacteria per infected cell. Complementation with panD restored replication ability, indicating that panD contributes to Salmonella replication in macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 are supported by gentamicin protection assays (Figure 2E) and immunofluorescence analysis (Figure 2F-G) with strong statistical significance (p<0.001 and p<0.0001). Claim C55 demonstrates genetic complementation, strengthening the conclusion. Claim C58 is a valid inference. The experiments include appropriate replicates (n=3 for in vitro, n=80 cells for microscopy) and proper controls.

results.result: The ΔpanD mutant showed normal growth rates in LB and RPMI media, indicating that the impaired intracellular replication was not due to a general growth defect.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60 are supported by growth curve data in Figure 2—figure supplements 1-2. This is an important control demonstrating that the intracellular replication defect is specific to the intracellular environment rather than a general fitness cost. The experiments include appropriate replicates (n=4).

results.result: The replication defect of ΔpanD in RAW264.7 cells was rescued by addition of 1 mM β-alanine to the culture medium.
results.evaluation: Claim C61 is supported by experimental data in Figure 2H. This is a critical experiment demonstrating that the replication defect is specifically due to β-alanine deficiency and can be complemented by exogenous β-alanine. The experiment includes appropriate replicates (n=3) and controls.

results.result: Replication of S. Typhi ΔpanD in human THP-1 macrophages was reduced by 2.6-fold compared to wild-type, suggesting that panD also facilitates S. Typhi replication within human macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 is supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 with statistical significance (p<0.01). Claim C63 is a reasonable inference. This extends the findings to another Salmonella serovar and human macrophages, strengthening the generalizability of the results. The experiment includes appropriate replicates (n=4).

results.result: β-alanine synthesis is critical for Salmonella replication inside macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claim C64 is a summary conclusion supported by multiple lines of evidence from claims C50-C63, including gene expression data, mutant phenotypes, complementation experiments, and rescue by exogenous β-alanine. The conclusion is well-supported by converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches.

results.result: The ΔpanD mutant showed dramatically attenuated virulence in mice with 100% survival over 10 days (vs. 0% for WT), significantly reduced bacterial burdens in liver and spleen, increased body weight, fewer bacteria per macrophage, and reduced liver pathology. Complementation restored virulence, demonstrating that β-alanine synthesis is critical for systemic Salmonella infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C78 are supported by comprehensive in vivo data in Figure 3B-F including survival curves (log-rank test, p<0.0001), bacterial burden measurements, body weight monitoring, immunofluorescence microscopy (n=80 cells), and histopathology. Claim C79 is a valid conclusion. The experiments include appropriate sample sizes (n=10 for survival, n=7 for bacterial burden), proper controls, and complementation strains. The dramatic phenotype (100% vs. 0% survival) provides strong evidence for the importance of β-alanine synthesis in virulence.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis revealed that mutation of panD caused extensive transcriptional changes (1379 differentially expressed genes) affecting multiple metabolic pathways including amino acid metabolism, lipid metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, energy metabolism, and nucleotide metabolism, indicating that β-alanine is involved in regulating diverse metabolic pathways in Salmonella.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 are supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 4A-D with appropriate statistical criteria (fold change ≥2, p<0.05) and biological replicates (n=3). PCA analysis shows clear separation between groups. GO and KEGG enrichment analyses are appropriate methods for interpreting the transcriptomic data. Claim C83 is a valid inference from these comprehensive data.

results.result: Mutation of panD decreased expression of genes involved in seven virulence-associated pathways (methionine metabolism, fatty acid β-oxidation, histidine biosynthesis, zinc/galactose/potassium/polyamine transport) and the transcriptional regulator LeuO. qRT-PCR validation of 16 selected genes confirmed downregulation in ΔpanD, and complementation restored expression to wild-type levels, confirming positive regulation by β-alanine.
results.evaluation: Claims C84, C87, C89 are supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 4E. Claims C90-C91 are supported by qRT-PCR validation in Figure 4F with statistical significance (p<0.05) and appropriate replicates (n=3). Claim C92 is a valid conclusion. The qRT-PCR validation of RNA-seq results and complementation experiments strengthen the findings. However, the functional significance of these pathways for virulence requires further investigation (addressed in subsequent experiments).

results.result: Expression of SPI-2 genes and other virulence-associated pathogenicity islands (SPI-1, SPI-3, SPI-4, SPI-5) was unaffected by panD mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 are supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 4—figure supplements 1-3. This is an important negative result indicating that β-alanine does not affect virulence through the major pathogenicity islands, suggesting alternative mechanisms. The data are clearly presented and appropriately analyzed.

results.result: β-alanine promotes Salmonella intracellular replication and virulence by activating virulence-associated pathways or the regulator LeuO, rather than by activating expression of virulence genes in pathogenicity islands.
results.evaluation: Claim C96 is a reasonable inference from the combined RNA-seq data showing downregulation of specific metabolic pathways (C84) and LeuO (C87) but no effect on SPI genes (C94-C95). However, this remains a hypothesis that requires functional validation of the specific pathways, which is addressed in subsequent experiments.

results.result: Mutations in genes involved in fatty acid β-oxidation (fadAB), methionine metabolism (metR), histidine biosynthesis (hisABCDFGHL), potassium uptake (kdpABC), galactose uptake (mglABC), polyamine uptake (potFGHI), and the transcriptional regulator leuO did not affect Salmonella colonization in mouse liver/spleen or body weight of infected mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C100 are supported by mouse infection data in Figure 5A-C with appropriate sample sizes (n=5 mice per group) and statistical analyses. These are important negative results indicating that these pathways, despite being downregulated in ΔpanD, do not individually account for the virulence defect. This narrows the focus to the remaining pathway (zinc transport).

results.result: Mutation of the zinc transporter gene znuA significantly decreased Salmonella colonization in mouse liver and spleen and increased body weight of infected mice, indicating that β-alanine might promote Salmonella virulence in vivo by promoting zinc uptake.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102 are supported by mouse infection data in Figure 5D with statistical significance (p<0.001) and appropriate sample sizes (n=5). The results are consistent with previous studies (cited). Claim C103 is a reasonable inference. This identifies zinc transport as a key pathway linking β-alanine to virulence.

results.result: Zinc concentration in macrophages of ΔpanD-infected mouse livers was 3.2-fold higher than in WT-infected mice, suggesting that panD and β-alanine are crucial for Salmonella to obtain zinc from host cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 is supported by experimental data in Figure 5E with strong statistical significance (p<0.0001) and appropriate sample size (n=5). Claim C105 is a reasonable inference. The accumulation of zinc in host cells when bacteria cannot take it up provides strong evidence for the role of β-alanine in zinc acquisition. However, the mechanism by which β-alanine affects zinc uptake requires further investigation.

results.result: The double mutant ΔpanDΔznuA showed significantly lower colonization and higher body weight in infected mice compared to the single mutant ΔznuA, suggesting that the contribution of panD to Salmonella virulence is partially dependent on znuA and that β-alanine promotes virulence partially by increasing zinc transporter gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 are supported by mouse infection data in Figure 5D with appropriate sample sizes (n=5) and statistical analyses. Claims C108-C109 are reasonable inferences from the epistasis analysis. The double mutant experiment is a strong genetic approach to test the relationship between panD and znuA. The use of "partially dependent" is appropriate since the double mutant shows an additive effect, indicating that panD has znuA-independent functions as well.

results.result: Zinc concentration in ΔpanD-infected RAW264.7 cells was 1.8-fold higher than in WT-infected cells, further indicating that panD and β-alanine are crucial for Salmonella to absorb zinc from macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claim C110 is supported by experimental data in Figure 6A with strong statistical significance (p<0.0001) and appropriate replicates (n=3). Claim C111 is a reasonable inference. This extends the in vivo zinc accumulation findings (C104) to the in vitro macrophage system, strengthening the conclusion.

results.result: Replication of the double mutant ΔpanDΔznuA in RAW264.7 cells was significantly reduced compared to the single mutant ΔznuA, implying that the contribution of panD to intracellular replication is partially dependent on znuA.
results.evaluation: Claim C112 is supported by experimental data in Figure 6B with appropriate replicates (n=3) and statistical analyses. Claim C113 is a reasonable inference from the epistasis analysis. This extends the in vivo epistasis findings (C106-C108) to the in vitro system, providing consistent evidence for the panD-znuA relationship.

results.result: Addition of 100 μM zinc rescued the replication defect of ΔpanD in RAW264.7 cells, while addition of 1 mM β-alanine did not rescue ΔznuA replication, suggesting that impaired replication due to β-alanine deficiency can be relieved by zinc supplementation.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C115 are supported by experimental data in Figure 6C-D with appropriate replicates (n=3) and statistical analyses. Claim C116 is a reasonable inference. These rescue experiments provide strong evidence for the epistatic relationship between β-alanine and zinc, supporting the model that β-alanine acts upstream of zinc uptake.

results.result: β-alanine promotes Salmonella replication within macrophages by increasing the expression of zinc transporter genes.
results.evaluation: Claim C117 is a summary conclusion supported by multiple lines of evidence including RNA-seq data showing znuABC downregulation in ΔpanD (C84), zinc accumulation in host cells infected with ΔpanD (C110), epistasis analysis with double mutants (C112-C113), and rescue experiments (C114-C116). The conclusion is well-supported by converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches.

results.result: Salmonella promotes its replication inside macrophages by utilizing both host- and bacterial-derived β-alanine, which promotes intracellular replication and systemic infection partially by increasing expression of zinc transporter genes and facilitating zinc uptake.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C119 are summary conclusions integrating findings from the entire study. The utilization of both host- and bacterial-derived β-alanine is supported by the metabolomics data (C29), supplementation experiments (C31-C33), and panD mutant phenotypes (C54-C79). The mechanism involving zinc transporter genes is supported by RNA-seq (C84), epistasis analysis (C106-C113), and rescue experiments (C114-C116). The use of "partially" is appropriate given the epistasis data showing znuA-independent effects.

results.result: Salmonella relies on a large amount of β-alanine to efficiently replicate in macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claim C120 is explicitly stated as speculation in the manuscript. While the importance of both host- and bacterial-derived β-alanine is demonstrated, the claim about requiring "a large amount" is not quantitatively supported. The dose-response experiment (C31-C32) shows effects at 1-4 mM, but whether this represents a "large amount" relative to other nutrients is not established. This remains a reasonable hypothesis but lacks direct quantitative evidence.

results.result: β-alanine increases expression of zinc transporter genes znuABC, representing an additional mechanism for efficient zinc uptake by Salmonella in macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claim C126 is supported by RNA-seq data (C84) showing downregulation of znuABC in ΔpanD, qRT-PCR validation (C90-C91), and functional evidence from zinc accumulation experiments (C104, C110). The characterization as an "additional mechanism" is appropriate given that ZnuABC function was previously known, but the regulation by β-alanine is novel.

results.result: Utilization of β-alanine promotes Salmonella uptake of zinc, which is required for metabolic needs and to subvert antimicrobial defense of macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claim C127 integrates findings from the current study (β-alanine promotes zinc uptake) with previous knowledge about zinc's roles in Salmonella pathogenesis (cited as C124). The first part (β-alanine promotes zinc uptake) is well-supported by the current data. The second part (zinc's functions) relies on prior literature, which is appropriately cited. This represents a valid synthesis of new and existing knowledge.

results.result: The panD gene is present in all Salmonella strains and its mutation markedly reduces replication in macrophages and virulence in mice, suggesting it may be a potential target to control systemic Salmonella infection.
results.evaluation: Claim C128 is stated as general knowledge about panD conservation. Claim C129 is a summary of experimental findings from the study (C54-C79). Claim C130 is explicitly stated as speculation about potential applications. While the conservation of panD and its importance for virulence support its potential as a therapeutic target, actual validation would require drug development and testing, which is beyond the scope of this study. The claim is appropriately framed as a possibility rather than a demonstrated fact.

results.result: Targeted metabolomics analysis of Salmonella-infected macrophages revealed that 8 out of 26 free amino acids showed significant differences in abundance, with β-alanine being downregulated in infected cells (claims C22-C25, C29).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question the metabolomics findings. One reviewer noted the work 'adds to the existing knowledge of metabolic flexibility displayed by STM during infection,' implicitly accepting the metabolomics data showing β-alanine changes.

results.result: Host-derived β-alanine facilitates Salmonella intracellular replication, as demonstrated by dose-dependent increases in bacterial replication with β-alanine supplementation (claims C30-C33, C37).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding without critique. One reviewer stated the work 'shows how Beta-alanine synthesis mediates zinc homeostasis regulation, possibly contributing to virulence,' and another noted β-alanine 'plays important roles in mediating STM infection and virulence,' supporting the conclusion that host-derived β-alanine facilitates replication.

results.result: Addition of β-alanine did not affect ROS/RNS levels or macrophage polarization (M1/M2 markers), indicating that β-alanine does not alter the macrophage immune response (claims C34-C36).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these control experiments. The acceptance of the overall mechanism implies acceptance of these controls showing β-alanine's effects are not mediated through altered macrophage immune responses.

results.result: CycA and GabP are not involved in β-alanine uptake in Salmonella, as demonstrated by mutant growth assays and infection experiments (claims C39-C42, C44-C45).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question these negative results. The overall acceptance of the ArgT transporter findings (discussed positively) implies acceptance of the exclusion of CycA and GabP as β-alanine transporters.

results.result: ArgT transports β-alanine in Salmonella, as shown by markedly decreased growth of the ΔargT mutant in minimal medium with β-alanine as the sole carbon source (claims C46-C47).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not critique this finding. The multidisciplinary approach was praised, and the identification of ArgT as a β-alanine transporter is part of the accepted mechanism linking β-alanine to Salmonella virulence.

results.result: panD expression is significantly enhanced during Salmonella growth inside macrophages and in N-minimal medium, suggesting a relationship between panD expression and intracellular growth (claims C50-C53).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding as part of the overall mechanism. One reviewer noted the work 'propose a mechanism by which panD, involved in B-Ala synthesis, mediates regulation of zinc homeostasis,' indicating acceptance of panD's role and its expression patterns.

results.result: The ΔpanD mutant shows impaired replication in macrophages (2.4-fold decrease at 20h), which is restored by complementation or β-alanine supplementation, demonstrating that panD contributes to intracellular replication (claims C54-C61).
results.evaluation: Reviewers found the results 'adequately supported by the authors' data' and noted the work is 'convincing.' The complementation and rescue experiments with β-alanine were not questioned, supporting the conclusion that panD is critical for intracellular replication.

results.result: panD also facilitates S. Typhi replication within human THP-1 macrophages, with a 2.6-fold reduction in replication for the ΔpanD mutant (claims C62-C63).
results.evaluation: One reviewer specifically noted 'by performing a small set of confirmatory experiments in S. Typhi, the authors provide some evidence of relevance to human infections,' explicitly supporting these findings and their significance.

results.result: β-alanine synthesis is critical for Salmonella replication inside macrophages (claim C64).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this conclusion. One stated the work 'shows how Beta-alanine synthesis mediates zinc homeostasis regulation, possibly contributing to virulence,' and another noted β-alanine 'plays important roles in mediating STM infection and virulence.'

results.result: β-alanine synthesis is critical for systemic Salmonella infection in mice, as demonstrated by improved survival, reduced bacterial burden, and decreased pathology in ΔpanD-infected mice compared to WT-infected mice (claims C67-C79).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the mouse infection data. One noted the authors 'employ a multidisciplinary approach that includes some mouse studies' and found the work 'convincing,' supporting the in vivo virulence findings.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis revealed that panD mutation causes extensive transcriptional changes (1379 differentially expressed genes) primarily affecting metabolic pathways, indicating β-alanine's involvement in regulating multiple metabolic processes (claims C80-C83).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question the RNA-seq findings. The acceptance of the proposed mechanism linking β-alanine to zinc transporter expression implies acceptance of the transcriptomic data supporting this pathway.

results.result: panD mutation decreased expression of genes in seven virulence-associated pathways (including zinc transport) and the regulator LeuO, with qRT-PCR validation confirming β-alanine's positive regulation of these pathways (claims C84, C87, C89-C92).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings as part of the mechanism. One reviewer noted the work 'shows how Beta-alanine synthesis mediates zinc homeostasis regulation,' directly supporting the finding that β-alanine regulates zinc transporter expression.

results.result: The expression of SPI-2 and other pathogenicity island genes (SPI-1, SPI-3, SPI-4, SPI-5) was unaffected by panD mutation (claims C94-C95).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these findings. The acceptance of the overall mechanism, which focuses on metabolic pathways rather than SPI gene expression, implies acceptance of these negative results.

results.result: β-alanine promotes Salmonella virulence by activating virulence-associated pathways or regulators like LeuO, rather than by activating pathogenicity island genes (claim C96).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this mechanistic interpretation. One noted the work 'shows how Beta-alanine synthesis mediates zinc homeostasis regulation, possibly contributing to virulence,' supporting the proposed mechanism through metabolic regulation rather than direct SPI activation.

results.result: Mutations in fadAB, metR, hisABCDFGHL, kdpABC, mglABC, potFGHI, and leuO did not affect Salmonella colonization or mouse body weight in infection assays (claims C97-C100).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question these negative results. The acceptance of the zinc transporter findings as the key mechanism implies acceptance of the exclusion of these other pathways as major contributors to the panD phenotype.

results.result: Mutation of znuA significantly decreased Salmonella colonization and increased mouse body weight, with zinc accumulation in ΔpanD-infected macrophages, indicating that β-alanine promotes virulence by facilitating zinc uptake (claims C101-C105).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this key mechanistic finding. One stated the work 'shows how Beta-alanine synthesis mediates zinc homeostasis regulation, possibly contributing to virulence,' directly supporting the link between β-alanine and zinc uptake as the mechanism for virulence.

results.result: The ΔpanDΔznuA double mutant showed greater attenuation than ΔznuA alone, indicating that panD's contribution to virulence is partially dependent on znuA and that β-alanine promotes virulence partially through zinc transporter expression (claims C106-C109).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this genetic epistasis analysis. The statement that 'results and model are adequately supported by the authors' data' indicates acceptance of the double mutant experiments supporting the proposed mechanism.

results.result: In vitro macrophage experiments confirmed that β-alanine promotes Salmonella replication by increasing zinc transporter expression, as shown by zinc accumulation in ΔpanD-infected cells, reduced replication of ΔpanDΔznuA, and rescue of ΔpanD by zinc supplementation (claims C110-C117).
results.evaluation: Reviewers found the results 'adequately supported' and the work 'convincing.' The in vitro validation of the zinc-dependent mechanism was not questioned, supporting the proposed pathway from β-alanine to zinc uptake to bacterial replication.

results.result: The overall model proposes that Salmonella utilizes both host- and bacterial-derived β-alanine to promote intracellular replication and systemic infection partially by increasing zinc transporter gene expression and zinc uptake (claims C118-C119, C126-C127).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly accepted this model. One stated 'the results and model are adequately supported by the authors' data,' and another noted the work 'shows how Beta-alanine synthesis mediates zinc homeostasis regulation, possibly contributing to virulence,' directly supporting the proposed mechanism.

results.result: The authors speculate that Salmonella relies on a large amount of β-alanine to efficiently replicate in macrophages (claim C120).
results.evaluation: This is explicitly stated as speculation by the authors. One reviewer noted 'further work will need to be performed to learn whether the Zn2+ functions as proposed in their mechanism,' suggesting some aspects of the model require additional validation, though this comment may relate more to mechanistic details than the overall importance of β-alanine.

results.result: The panD gene may be used as a potential target to control systemic Salmonella infection, given that it is present in all Salmonella strains and its mutation markedly reduces virulence (claims C129-C130).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this translational implication. The acceptance of the virulence data and the statement that the work is 'valuable' and 'convincing' support the potential therapeutic relevance of targeting panD.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on metabolomics findings (C22-C25, C29). Both evaluations support the LC-MS/MS data showing β-alanine changes during infection. Peer reviewers implicitly accepted these findings as part of the overall mechanism.
Complete agreement on host-derived β-alanine facilitating bacterial replication (C30-C33, C37). Both evaluations support the dose-dependent supplementation data and its implications for virulence.
Full agreement on control experiments (C34-C36) showing β-alanine effects are not mediated through altered macrophage immune responses (ROS/RNS, M1/M2 polarization).

Both support the exclusion of CycA as a β-alanine transporter (C39-C42). OpenEval provides detailed assessment of individual experiments; peer reviewers accepted these negative results as part of the overall transporter identification.
Both support the exclusion of GabP as a β-alanine transporter (C44-C45). OpenEval evaluates this separately; peer reviewers grouped it with other transporter findings.
Complete agreement on ArgT as the β-alanine transporter (C46-C47). Both evaluations support this finding, though OpenEval notes complementation experiments would strengthen the conclusion.
Full agreement on panD expression patterns (C50-C53). Both support the qRT-PCR and reporter data showing panD upregulation in intracellular conditions.

Strong agreement on panD's role in intracellular replication (C54-C58). Both evaluations support the gentamicin protection assays and complementation data. OpenEval provides detailed statistical assessment; peer reviewers found the work 'convincing.'

Both support the control experiments (C59-C60) showing no growth defect in rich medium. OpenEval evaluates this separately; peer reviewers accepted it as part of the intracellular replication findings.
Agreement on β-alanine rescue experiments (C61). Both evaluations support this critical demonstration that exogenous β-alanine complements the replication defect.
Perfect agreement on S. Typhi validation (C62-C63). Peer reviewers specifically praised these confirmatory experiments in human macrophages as providing evidence of relevance to human infections.

Complete agreement on the summary conclusion (C64) that bacterial-derived β-alanine is critical for intracellular replication. Both evaluations support this integration of multiple experimental lines.

Full agreement on in vivo virulence findings (C67-C79). Both evaluations support the dramatic mouse infection phenotypes. OpenEval provides detailed statistical assessment; peer reviewers found the multidisciplinary approach 'convincing.'
Complete agreement on RNA-seq findings (C80-C83). Both evaluations support the transcriptomic data and pathway analyses identifying metabolic changes in ΔpanD.
Full agreement on zinc transporter downregulation (C84, C87, C89-C92). Both evaluations support the RNA-seq and qRT-PCR validation showing β-alanine regulates znuABC expression.
Agreement on negative results (C94-C95) showing no effect on SPI genes. Both evaluations accept these findings as important for narrowing the mechanism to metabolic pathways.
Complete agreement on mechanistic interpretation (C96) that β-alanine affects virulence through metabolic regulation rather than SPI activation. Both support this conclusion from the RNA-seq data.
Full agreement on negative results (C97-C100) excluding other downregulated pathways as major contributors. Both evaluations accept these findings as narrowing focus to zinc transport.
Strong agreement on zinc transport as key pathway (C101-C103). Both evaluations support the mouse infection data identifying znuA as critical for the mechanism.
Agreement on zinc accumulation findings (C104-C105). Both evaluations support the data showing zinc accumulates in host cells when bacteria cannot take it up.
Complete agreement on epistasis analysis (C106-C109). Both evaluations support the double mutant experiments showing panD's virulence role is partially dependent on znuA.
Agreement on in vitro zinc accumulation (C110-C111). Both evaluations support this extension of in vivo findings to the macrophage system.
Agreement on in vitro epistasis (C112-C113). Both evaluations support the consistency between in vitro and in vivo epistasis analyses.
Agreement on rescue experiments (C114-C116). Both evaluations support the epistatic relationship demonstrated by zinc and β-alanine supplementation.
Agreement on summary conclusion (C117) linking β-alanine to zinc uptake. Both evaluations support this integration of multiple experimental approaches.

Strong agreement on the overall mechanism (C118-C119). Both evaluations support the model integrating host- and bacterial-derived β-alanine with zinc transporter regulation. Peer reviewers found the model 'adequately supported.'

Both evaluations rate this as UNCERTAIN (C120). OpenEval notes lack of quantitative evidence for 'large amount' claim; peer reviewers suggest further work needed on mechanistic details. Both appropriately recognize this as speculation.
Agreement on β-alanine regulation of zinc uptake as an additional mechanism (C126). Both evaluations support this novel finding while acknowledging prior knowledge of ZnuABC function.
Agreement on the integrated model (C127) linking β-alanine-mediated zinc uptake to known zinc functions in pathogenesis. Both evaluations support this synthesis of new and existing knowledge.

Agreement on therapeutic implications (C129-C130). Both evaluations support the potential relevance while appropriately recognizing this as speculation requiring further validation. Peer reviewers found the work 'valuable.'
